topics: 🙏 God Prays — 'the house of My prayer' and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha's blessing in the Holy of Holies
⏱️ A Moment of Anger — how long God's anger lasts, Balaam's secret, and the rooster's crest
🐓 Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and the Heretic — why he fell asleep and learned not to curse
⚖️ Moses' Three Requests — why the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper
🌿 Firsts in Torah — Abraham calls God 'Lord', Leah gives thanks, and the meaning of Reuben and Ruth
😤 Provoking the Wicked — when it is permitted and when the hour smiles upon them

overview.title: 📖 Overview: God Prays, God's Anger, and Moses' Questions
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: יְהִי רָצוֹן מִלְּפָנַי שֶׁיִּכְבְּשׁוּ רַחֲמַי אֶת כַּעֲסִי
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: This daf is a chain of aggadic teachings of Rabbi Yoḥanan, first in the name of Rabbi Yosei and then in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai. It opens with the startling idea that God Himself prays — that His mercy overcome His anger — and that He asked Rabbi Yishmael the High Priest for a blessing. From there it explores how brief God's anger is, why Balaam's curses failed, and the lesson Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi learned when he tried to curse a heretic. Moses' three requests lead to the classic question of why the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper. The second amud turns to Abraham calling God 'Lord', Leah's thanksgiving, the meaning of the names Reuben and Ruth, the pain of wayward children, whether one may provoke the wicked, and the value of fixing a place for prayer and serving Torah scholars.

slides.title: 🙏 Does God Pray? And What Does He Pray?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei opens the daf

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, prays? Isaiah 56:7 says בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי, 'the house of My prayer', not 'the house of their prayer'.

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: 'May it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger, that My mercy prevail over My other attributes, that I conduct Myself with My children with the attribute of mercy, and that I enter before them beyond the letter of the law.'

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha entered the Holy of Holies to offer incense and saw Akatriel Ya, Lord of Hosts, on a high and exalted throne. He said: 'Yishmael, My son, bless Me!'

lines.speaker: R' Yishmael
lines.text: 'May it be Your will that Your mercy overcome Your anger… and that You enter before them beyond the letter of the law.' And God nodded His head.

lines.speaker: Lesson
lines.text: שֶׁלֹּא תְּהֵא בִּרְכַּת הֶדְיוֹט קַלָּה בְּעֵינֶיךָ — do not take the blessing of an ordinary person lightly.

callout.label: Big idea:
callout.text: God's own 'prayer' is a wish that mercy win out over strict justice. If God accepts a human blessing, all the more so must we value one another's blessings.

slides.title: ⏱️ How Long Is God Angry, and Who Can Find That Moment?
slides.subtitle: 'God is furious every day' (Psalms 7:12) — but only for a rega

nodes.content: ❓ Is there really anger before the Holy One? Yes: 'God is furious every day' (Psalms 7:12)
⏱️ How long? A moment (רֶגַע) — 1/58,888 of an hour; Rabbi Avin: as long as it takes to say the word. Proof: 'His anger is but for a moment' (Psalms 30:6)
🔮 No creature can pinpoint that moment except Balaam the wicked — 'who knows the knowledge of the Most High' (Numbers 24:16)

columns.label: Objection
columns.content: He could not even know the mind of his donkey — did he know the mind of the Most High?

columns.label: Answer
columns.content: It means only that he could time the instant God is angry, and curse at that moment

nodes.content: ✅ Rabbi Elazar: 'Know the righteous acts of the Lord' (Micah 6:5) — God did not become angry at all in the days of Balaam, so the curse failed: 'How can I condemn whom God has not condemned?' (Numbers 23:8)

callout.label: When is it?
callout.text: Abaye: in the first three hours of the day, when the rooster's crest turns white and it stands on one leg with no red streaks in its crest. Rabbi Meir: it is the moment the kings of East and West put on their crowns and bow to the sun.

slides.title: 🐓 Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi Tries to Curse a Heretic
slides.subtitle: A story that ends in a different lesson than it began with
slides.hebrewSource: כִּי מְטָא הַהִיא שַׁעְתָּא — נָיֵים. אֲמַר: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא לְמֶעְבַּד הָכִי
slides.label: The story:
slides.text: A heretic in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's neighborhood kept tormenting him with challenges to verses. One day he tied a rooster between the legs of his bed and watched it, planning to curse the heretic at the exact moment of God's anger. When the moment came — he had dozed off. He concluded: it is not proper conduct to do this, even to the wicked. 'His mercy is over all His creations' (Psalms 145:9), and 'Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good' (Proverbs 17:26). The same daf adds Rabbi Yoḥanan's teaching that a single pang of remorse in the heart is better than many lashes (Hosea 2:9), and Reish Lakish: better than a hundred lashes, for 'a rebuke enters deeper into a man of understanding than a hundred lashes to a fool' (Proverbs 17:10).

slides.title: ⚖️ Moses' Three Requests and the Righteous Who Suffer
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei: all three were granted; Rabbi Meir: only two
rows: That the Divine Presence rest upon Israel
'Is it not in that You go with us' (Exodus 33:16)
That the Divine Presence not rest upon the nations
'So that we are distinguished, I and Your people' (Exodus 33:16)
To know God's ways — why the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper
R' Yoḥanan: yes; R' Meir: no — 'I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious' (Exodus 33:19)
First answer: righteous who prospers = righteous son of a righteous man
Rejected: 'children shall not be put to death for the fathers' (Deut. 24:16) — ancestors' sins count only when one adopts their deeds
Final answer: prospering righteous = completely righteous; suffering righteous = not completely righteous; prospering wicked = not completely wicked; suffering wicked = completely wicked

callout.label: Seeing God's back:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa: 'You cannot see My face' (Exodus 33:20) — when I wanted at the burning bush, you did not; now that you want, I do not. Rabbi Yonatan disagrees: for hiding his face Moses earned a glowing countenance, for 'fearing' Israel feared to approach him, for not 'gazing' he beheld the likeness of the Lord. What did he see? Rav Ḥana bar Bizna: the knot of God's tefillin. And every good promise of God is fulfilled — 'I will make from you a mighty nation' came true through Reḥaviya's very many descendants.

slides.title: 😤 May One Provoke the Wicked?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai says yes; Rabbi Yitzḥak says no — the Gemara offers three resolutions

boxes.title: Permitted to provoke
items: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai and the baraita of Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Matun
'The keepers of the Torah will fight them' (Proverbs 28:4)
'Do not compete with evil-doers' (Psalms 37:1) means only: do not become like them
Only one whose own conscience troubles him says otherwise

boxes.title: Do not provoke
items: Rabbi Yitzḥak: if the hour is smiling on a wicked man, do not provoke him
He even wins in judgment and sees his enemies fall
Rav Huna: the wicked 'swallows the man more righteous than he' (Habakkuk 1:13) — but not the completely righteous

boxes.title: Three resolutions
items: 1️⃣ Personal matters: don't provoke; matters of Heaven: do
2️⃣ Both about Heaven: provoke only when the hour is not smiling on him
3️⃣ Both when the hour smiles: a completely righteous person may; one not completely righteous may not
Or: when the hour smiles on the wicked, even the righteous can be harmed

callout.label: Also on 7b:
callout.text: Abraham was the first to call God 'Lord' (Genesis 15:8), and Daniel's prayer was answered 'for the sake of the Lord' — for Abraham's sake. Leah was the first to thank God ('This time I will give thanks', Genesis 29:35). Reuben = 'See the difference between my son and my father-in-law's son' Esau. Ruth = she merited David, who inundated God with song. Wayward children at home are harder than the war of Gog and Magog. One who fixes a place for prayer sees his enemies fall (II Samuel 7:10), and serving Torah is greater than studying it — Elisha 'poured water' over Elijah's hands (II Kings 3:11).

summary.principle: God's own prayer is that mercy overcome anger — and this daf teaches people to imitate that: value every blessing, do not curse even the wicked, and accept remorse over punishment.

flowSteps.content: 🙏 God prays: 'May My mercy overcome My anger' — and asked Rabbi Yishmael for that very blessing
⏱️ God's anger lasts only a rega; only Balaam could time it, and in his days God was not angry at all
🐓 Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi slept through the moment → 'His mercy is over all His creations'; a pang of remorse beats a hundred lashes

columns.content: ⚖️ Moses' three requests: Shekhina on Israel, not on the nations, and (per R' Yoḥanan) why the righteous suffer — the completely righteous prosper
😤 Provoking the wicked: permitted for matters of Heaven, when the hour is not smiling on them, or by the completely righteous

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Fix a place for prayer and your enemies fall; serving Torah scholars is greater than study itself

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei derive that God prays?
o: From God asking Rabbi Yishmael to bless Him
From Isaiah 56:7, which says 'the house of My prayer' rather than 'the house of their prayer'
From 'God is furious every day' (Psalms 7:12)
From Moses' request 'Show me Your ways'
quiz.e: The verse says 'the house of My prayer' (בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי), implying that God Himself prays. Rabbi Yishmael's story is a supporting baraita, not the source of the derivation.

quiz.q: What lesson did Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi draw when he fell asleep at the moment of God's anger?
o: That the rooster is not a reliable sign of God's anger
That Balaam alone could find that moment
That it is not proper conduct to curse people, even the wicked, since 'His mercy is over all His creations'
That one should pray at sunrise before the kings bow to the sun
quiz.e: He concluded from his nodding off that it is improper to curse even a heretic, citing Psalms 145:9 and 'Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good' (Proverbs 17:26).

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's final explanation, who is 'the righteous person who suffers'?
o: A righteous person who is the son of a wicked person
A completely righteous person being tested
A righteous person who is not completely righteous
A wicked person who is the son of a righteous person
quiz.e: The first explanation (son of a wicked father) is rejected because children are punished for ancestors only when they adopt their deeds. The Gemara concludes the sufferer is a righteous person who is not completely righteous.

quiz.q: On which of Moses' three requests do Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Meir disagree?
o: Whether the Divine Presence would rest upon Israel
Whether the Divine Presence would not rest upon the nations
Whether God revealed to Moses the ways in which He conducts the world
Whether Moses could see God's face
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir holds two requests were granted and one was not: God did not reveal His ways, as it says 'I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious' (Exodus 33:19), even to one who is not worthy.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the tension between 'the keepers of the Torah will fight them' and Rabbi Yitzḥak's 'do not provoke a wicked person upon whom the hour is smiling'?
o: It rules entirely like Rabbi Yitzḥak: never provoke the wicked
It distinguishes personal matters from matters of Heaven, whether the hour is smiling, and whether the provoker is completely righteous
It says Rabbi Yitzḥak referred only to heretics
It says Proverbs 28:4 refers to the World-to-Come
quiz.e: The Gemara offers several resolutions: one may provoke in matters of Heaven but not personal matters; or only a wicked person on whom the hour is not smiling; or only a completely righteous person may provoke one on whom the hour smiles.
